title: Futility of Futilities
subtitle: Ecclesiastes 1:1–18
description: The Teacher states his verdict, watches the world's circles, and reports his first experiment: wisdom itself.
paragraphs: The book opens by introducing its speaker and his verdict in the same breath: “These are the words of the Teacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem.” Then the verdict itself, in two pieces: “Futility of futilities,” “futility of futilities! Everything is futile!” This is not a story of things that happened to the Teacher. It is his argument, the record of a man who set out to test everything he could reach and kept arriving at that word. His question is the working question of the whole book: “What does a man gain from all his labor, at which he toils under the sun?” Everything he says is said under the sun, inside this life's limits, and he marks the boundary himself.

His first evidence is the world's motion, which goes everywhere and arrives nowhere. “Generations come and generations go, but the earth remains forever.” The people change; the stage does not. “The sun rises and the sun sets; it hurries back to where it rises.” The wind circles south and north and back again. “All the rivers flow into the sea, yet the sea is never full,” and the streams return to where they came from and flow again. The watcher tires before the world does: “All things are wearisome, more than one can describe; the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear content with hearing.” Nature is not empty to the Teacher. It is full, busy, and going in circles.

From the circles he draws his famous conclusion: “What has been will be again, and what has been done will be done again;” “there is nothing new under the sun.” When someone points at a thing and calls it new, the Teacher answers that it existed in the ages before us, and the ages before us are themselves forgotten: “There is no remembrance of those who came before, and those yet to come will not be remembered by those who follow after.” Memory fails in both directions, backward and forward. The new is old, the old is lost, and the man watching it all is on his way to being lost the same way.

Then the Teacher begins his experiments, and wisdom is the first thing he tests. “I, the Teacher, was king over Israel in Jerusalem.” “And I set my mind to seek and explore by wisdom all that is done under heaven.” His early judgment on the assignment itself is bleak: “What a miserable task God has laid upon the sons of men to occupy them!” What he found under the sun, he found everywhere the same: “I have seen all the things that are done under the sun, and have found them all to be futile, a pursuit of the wind.” The crooked stays crooked under examination: “What is crooked cannot be straightened, and what is lacking cannot be counted.”

His credentials for the test are stated without modesty: “Behold, I have grown and increased in wisdom beyond all those before me who were over Jerusalem, and my mind has observed a wealth of wisdom and knowledge.” He turned the same mind to madness and folly for comparison, and the comparison itself failed him: “So I set my mind to know wisdom and madness and folly; I learned that this, too, is a pursuit of the wind.” The chapter's last line is the cost of the whole education, and the book will not let the reader unhear it: “For with much wisdom comes much sorrow, and as knowledge grows, grief increases.” The wisest man in Jerusalem has finished his first test. What it gave him was more to grieve over. His next tests are pleasure and building, and he runs them at full royal scale.

title: The Test of Pleasure and Work
subtitle: Ecclesiastes 2:1–26
description: Pleasure, building, and greatness are tested at royal scale, and the first joy refrain answers the despair.
paragraphs: The Teacher's next experiment is pleasure, run deliberately, like a test rather than a binge: “Come now, I will test you with pleasure; enjoy what is good!” The result came back at once: “But it proved to be futile.” Laughter got its own verdict, and pleasure got a question it could not answer: “What does it accomplish?” Even wine was taken on methodically, as an instrument rather than an escape: “I sought to cheer my body with wine and to embrace folly,” with “my mind still guiding me with wisdom,” to see what was worthwhile for men to do during the few days of their lives. The most disciplined pleasure-seeking in Jerusalem found nothing at the end of it.

Then he built. “I expanded my pursuits. I built houses and planted vineyards for myself.” Gardens and parks followed, with every kind of fruit tree, and reservoirs to water the groves. Servants were bought and born in his house; herds and flocks passed everyone before him; silver and gold and the treasure of kings came in; singers were gathered, and the delights of the sons of men. His own summary is a king's balance sheet: “So I became great and surpassed all in Jerusalem who had preceded me; and my wisdom remained with me.” His appetite was given an unlimited budget: “Anything my eyes desired, I did not deny myself. I refused my heart no pleasure.”

Then came the reckoning, and it is the hinge of the chapter: “Yet when I considered all the works that my hands had accomplished and what I had toiled to achieve, I found everything to be futile, a pursuit of the wind; there was nothing to be gained under the sun.” He turned from building to the comparison that had failed him in chapter 1, wisdom against folly, and this time the comparison held, up to a point: “And I saw that wisdom exceeds folly, just as light exceeds darkness.” “The wise man has eyes in his head, but the fool walks in darkness.” Then the point past which it would not go: “Yet I also came to realize that one fate overcomes them both.”

Death is the fact that breaks the comparison. “For there is no lasting remembrance of the wise, just as with the fool, seeing that both will be forgotten in the days to come.” “Alas, the wise man will die just like the fool!” The Teacher's response is not composure: “So I hated life, because the work that is done under the sun was grievous to me.” And what he built turned on him from the other direction, the future: “I hated all for which I had toiled under the sun, because I must leave it to the man who comes after me.” “And who knows whether that man will be wise or foolish?” A lifetime of skilled labor, handed to a stranger whose quality is a coin toss: “So my heart began to despair over all the labor that I had done under the sun.”

Out of the despair comes the book's first refrain, the conclusion the Teacher will reach again and again: “Nothing is better for a man than to eat and drink and enjoy his work. I have also seen that this is from the hand of God.” “For apart from Him, who can eat and who can find enjoyment?” Enjoyment itself turns out to be a gift rather than an achievement: to the man pleasing in God's sight He gives wisdom and knowledge and joy, “but to the sinner He assigns the task of gathering and accumulating that which he will hand over to one who pleases God.” The accumulator works for someone else either way. The Teacher's tests have now failed at wisdom, pleasure, and greatness. What he does next is stop testing and start watching: the seasons, the courts, the beasts, and the grave.

title: A Time for Everything
subtitle: Ecclesiastes 3:1–22
description: The seasons poem stands whole, eternity sits in the heart, and man and beast go to one dust.
paragraphs: The Teacher's watching begins with the book's most famous poem, and it is given here whole, in the order he wrote it: “To everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven:” “a time to be born and a time to die, a time to plant and a time to uproot, a time to kill and a time to heal, a time to break down and a time to build, a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance, a time to cast away stones and a time to gather stones together, a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing, a time to search and a time to count as lost, a time to keep and a time to discard, a time to tear and a time to mend, a time to be silent and a time to speak, a time to love and a time to hate, a time for war and a time for peace.” Birth and death get equal lines. So do killing and healing, weeping and dancing, war and peace. The poem does not sort the times into good and bad. It says they come.

Under the poem stands the Teacher's explanation of the ache people feel inside it: “He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in the hearts of men, yet they cannot fathom the work that God has done from beginning to end.” Eternity in the heart, and no view of the whole: that is the human position as he states it. His refrain follows inside the same movement: “I know that there is nothing better for them than to rejoice and do good while they live,” “and also that every man should eat and drink and find satisfaction in all his labor,” “this is the gift of God.” Satisfaction is named a gift here, not a wage. And permanence belongs to God's side of the line: “I know that everything God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it or taken from it. God does it so that they should fear Him.”

Then he looks at the courts, and the seasons turn ugly: “Furthermore, I saw under the sun that in the place of judgment there is wickedness, and in the place of righteousness there is wickedness.” Wickedness sitting in both chairs is the observation. His answer to himself is a time he cannot see: “God will judge the righteous and the wicked, since there is a time for every activity and every deed.” He says it in his heart, as a conviction held against the evidence in front of him, and the chapter moves on without the scene changing.

Next he tests men against beasts, and states the result as plainly as anything in the book: “As for the sons of men, God tests them so that they may see for themselves that they are but beasts.” “For the fates of both men and beasts are the same: As one dies, so dies the other,” and “they all have the same breath.” “Man has no advantage over the animals, since everything is futile.” “All go to one place; all come from dust, and all return to dust.” Then the Teacher does something his argument rarely does. He leaves a question open instead of closing it: “Who knows if the spirit of man rises upward and the spirit of the animal descends into the earth?” It stands in the text unanswered, in the middle of his bleakest paragraph.

The chapter ends with the refrain again, now tied to the dust: “I have seen that there is nothing better for a man than to enjoy his work, because that is his lot. For who can bring him to see what will come after him?” A man's lot is his work and his enjoyment of it now, because the future after him is sealed from his sight. The seasons turn, the courts stay crooked, the dust waits for man and beast alike, and the Teacher's prescription is the same one he reached at the end of his building test. Eat, drink, enjoy the work. It is the gift of God, and it does not wait for the argument to resolve.

title: Two Are Better Than One
subtitle: Ecclesiastes 4:1–16
description: Oppression without a comforter, envy as the engine of toil, and the threefold cord against the lone man.
paragraphs: The watching turns from seasons to people, and the first sight is the worst in the book so far: “Again I looked, and I considered all the oppression taking place under the sun. I saw the tears of the oppressed, and they had no comforter; the power lay in the hands of their oppressors, and there was no comforter.” The phrase lands twice, once for each side of the power. His conclusion shocks on purpose: “So I admired the dead, who had already died, above the living, who are still alive.” “But better than both is he who has not yet existed, who has not seen the evil that is done under the sun.” This is the Teacher under his own limiter, reporting what oppression looks like from inside a world where no comforter comes. The text does not interrupt him to soften it.

From oppression he moves to the engine underneath ordinary work: “I saw that all labor and success spring from a man’s envy of his neighbor.” A man does not toil simply to live; he toils to keep up, and the Teacher calls the whole arrangement “a pursuit of the wind.” The opposite pole is no better: “The fool folds his hands and consumes his own flesh.” Between envy and idleness sits his small, calm preference: “Better one handful with tranquility than two handfuls with toil and pursuit of the wind.” One handful, and peace with it, beats both hands full and the wind for wages.

Then a portrait, one of the saddest in the book: “There is a man all alone, without even a son or brother. And though there is no end to his labor, his eyes are still not content with his wealth.” The Teacher puts the question in the man's own mouth, the question the man apparently never asks himself: “For whom do I toil and bereave my soul of enjoyment?” No heir, no partner, no friend, and no enjoyment either; the work feeds only itself. The Teacher's verdict is short: “This too is futile,” “a miserable task.”

Against the lone man stands the book's warmest saying: “Two are better than one, because they have a good return for their labor.” “For if one falls down, his companion can lift him up; but pity the one who falls without another to help him up!” Two lying down keep warm; one cannot. Two can resist an attacker who would overpower one. Then the saying widens past pairs into the image everyone remembers: “Moreover, a cord of three strands is not quickly broken.” Companionship in this book is not decoration. It is the Teacher's practical answer to falls, cold, and attack, set in the middle of a chapter about tears and envy.

The chapter closes at the palace, with a changing of the guard: “Better is a poor but wise youth than an old but foolish king who no longer knows how to take a warning.” The youth comes from prison to the throne, the crowds follow him, the old king is replaced. And then the Teacher watches the replacement age into the same story: the people who come later will not celebrate the successor either. “There is no limit to all the people who were before them. Yet the successor will not be celebrated by those who come even later.” Fame at the top is a season like the rest. The chapter that began with tears ends with a throne no one will remember, and the argument turns next to the house of God and the danger of many words.

title: Guard Your Steps
subtitle: Ecclesiastes 5:1–6:12
description: Few words before God, vows paid, money that never satisfies, and wealth a stranger enjoys.
paragraphs: The argument turns toward worship, and the Teacher's counsel is restraint: “Guard your steps when you go to the house of God. Draw near to listen rather than to offer the sacrifice of fools, who do not know that they do wrong.” Listening outranks speaking in God's house, because of where each party stands: “Do not be quick to speak, and do not be hasty in your heart to utter a word before God. For God is in heaven and you are on earth. So let your words be few.” Many words are the fool's sacrifice, in prayer as in dreams: words multiply, and futility multiplies with them.

Vows get the same treatment, and it is not gentle: “When you make a vow to God, do not delay in fulfilling it, because He takes no pleasure in fools. Fulfill your vow.” “It is better not to vow than to make a vow and not fulfill it.” A mouth can make the flesh sin, and explaining to the messenger that the vow was a mistake will not retrieve it. The section's sum is blunt: “For as many dreams bring futility, so do many words. Therefore, fear God.” Under the Teacher's sun, even religion is a place where a man can ruin himself with his own mouth.

Then back to the province, where oppression turns out to have a chain of command: one official watched by a superior, and others higher still over them, and the king himself profiting from the fields. Money, though, is the chapter's deep subject: “He who loves money is never satisfied by money, and he who loves wealth is never satisfied by income.” Goods increase and consumers increase with them, until the owner's whole profit is watching. Sleep itself takes sides: “The sleep of the worker is sweet, whether he eats little or much, but the abundance of the rich man permits him no sleep.”

The darkest case follows: “There is a grievous evil I have seen under the sun: wealth hoarded to the harm of its owner,” or lost in a failed venture just when a son needs an inheritance. The exit cancels the accumulation: “As a man came from his mother’s womb, so he will depart again, naked as he arrived. He takes nothing for his labor to carry in his hands.” The hoarder's whole story, told in one direction: born naked, eats in darkness with sorrow and anger, departs exactly as he came, having toiled for the wind.

Against that case the Teacher sets his refrain at its fullest: “Here is what I have seen to be good and fitting: to eat and drink, and to find satisfaction in all the labor one does under the sun during the few days of life that God has given him,” “for this is his lot.” Riches themselves are not condemned. God gives some men riches “and He has enabled him to enjoy them, to accept his lot, and to rejoice in his labor. This is a gift from God.” Chapter 6 shows the gift withheld: “God gives a man riches, wealth, and honor, so that he lacks nothing his heart desires; but God does not allow him to enjoy them. Instead, a stranger will enjoy them.” A hundred children, two thousand years, no enjoyment, and a stillborn is better off. The appetite outlasts everything: “All a man’s labor is for his mouth, yet his appetite is never satisfied.” And the section ends on the question no one under the sun can answer for another: “For who knows what is good for a man during the few days in which he passes through his fleeting life like a shadow?”

title: Better the House of Mourning
subtitle: Ecclesiastes 7:1–29
description: The better sayings, prosperity and adversity from one hand, and the search that could not fathom.
paragraphs: Chapter 7 turns to sayings, and they open with the chapter 3 poem turned sober: “A good name is better than fine perfume, and one’s day of death is better than his day of birth.” “It is better to enter a house of mourning than a house of feasting, since death is the end of every man, and the living should take this to heart.” “Sorrow is better than laughter, for a sad countenance is good for the heart.” The wise keep their hearts where the funerals are; fools keep theirs in the house of pleasure. Even correction is priced by its pain: “It is better to heed a wise man’s rebuke than to listen to the song of fools.” A fool's laughter is thorns crackling under a pot, loud and quick and gone.

The sayings continue through conduct. Extortion makes a wise man a fool and a bribe corrupts the heart. “The end of a matter is better than the beginning, and a patient spirit is better than a proud one.” Anger settles in the lap of fools, and nostalgia is refused as a question: “Why were the old days better than these?” “For it is unwise of you to ask about this.” Wisdom is ranked with money as shelter, and then past it: “For wisdom, like money, is a shelter, and the advantage of knowledge is that wisdom preserves the life of its owner.” Money shelters a man's goods. Wisdom shelters the man.

Then the chapter looks up: “Consider the work of God: Who can straighten what He has bent?” Prosperity and adversity are a matched pair from the same hand: “In the day of prosperity, be joyful, but in the day of adversity, consider this: God has made one of these along with the other, so that a man cannot discover anything that will come after him.” What the Teacher saw inside his futile life breaks the moral arithmetic his readers keep trying to run: “A righteous man perishing in his righteousness, and a wicked man living long in his wickedness.” His counsel from that sight is the book's most argued pair of lines, given here as printed: “Do not be overly righteous, and do not make yourself too wise. Why should you destroy yourself?” “Do not be excessively wicked, and do not be a fool. Why should you die before your time?” His own summary holds both warnings in one hand: “For he who fears God will follow both warnings.”

Wisdom's strength is real, and so is its owner's failure: “Wisdom makes the wise man stronger than ten rulers in a city.” “Surely there is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins.” The Teacher turns the test on himself, and the report is honest: “All this I tested by wisdom,” resolving, “I resolve to be wise.” “But it was beyond me.” “What exists is out of reach and very deep. Who can fathom it?” The man who explored everything under the sun reports a depth he could not reach.

His last search in the chapter is the bitter one, and it is told here as he told it, as his own accounting: “And I find more bitter than death the woman who is a snare, whose heart is a net, and whose hands are chains. The man who pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is ensnared.” He describes his method, adding one thing to another to find an explanation, and his finding: “among a thousand I have found one upright man, but among all these I have not found one such woman.” The chapter's actual conclusion is not about women. It is about everyone: “Only this have I found: I have discovered that God made mankind upright, but they have sought out many schemes.” Upright at the making, scheming ever since, is the Teacher's verdict on the whole species, himself included in the search that failed.

title: Time and Chance Happen to Them All
subtitle: Ecclesiastes 8:1–9:18
description: The wicked praised at their graves, the great inversion, one fate for all, and the forgotten poor wise man.
paragraphs: The Teacher addresses life under a king, and wisdom is still worth having there: “Who is like the wise man? Who knows the interpretation of a matter? A man’s wisdom brightens his face, and the sternness of his face is changed.” His counsel is obedience with an oath behind it: “Keep the king’s command, I say, because of your oath before God.” The king's word is supreme, and the subject's oldest question hangs unanswered: “What are you doing?” A wise heart knows the right time and procedure, but time itself is not in human hands: “As no man has power over the wind to contain it, so no one has authority over his day of death.” No discharge in wartime, no release for the wicked from their wickedness.

Then an observation that still stings: “Then too, I saw the burial of the wicked who used to go in and out of the holy place, and they were praised in the city where they had done so.” Wicked men, honored at the grave, praised where they did their deeds. Slow justice feeds the problem: “When the sentence for a crime is not speedily executed, the hearts of men become fully set on doing evil.” A sinner can do evil a hundred times and live long. Against all of it the Teacher states what he also knows, and lets both stand: “yet I also know that it will go well with those who fear God, who are reverent in His presence.” The wicked who do not fear God will not fare well, and their days will not lengthen like a shadow. He does not reconcile the graveyard praise with the promise. He reports them side by side.

Chapter 8 ends with the inversion named outright and the refrain answering it: “There are righteous men who get what the actions of the wicked deserve, and there are wicked men who get what the actions of the righteous deserve. I say that this too is futile.” “So I commended the enjoyment of life, because there is nothing better for a man under the sun than to eat and drink and be merry.” Behind both stands his closing admission for the chapter: he applied his mind day and night, “and that a man is unable to comprehend the work that is done under the sun.” “Despite his efforts to search it out, he cannot find its meaning; even if the wise man claims to know, he is unable to comprehend.”

Chapter 9 gathers the whole argument into one fate: “So I took all this to heart and concluded that the righteous and the wise, as well as their deeds, are in God’s hands.” What lies ahead, love or hate, no man knows. “It is the same for all: There is a common fate for the righteous and the wicked, for the good and the bad, for the clean and the unclean.” The hearts of men are full of evil and madness while they live, “and afterward they join the dead.” Yet life itself still holds one advantage: “There is hope, however, for anyone who is among the living; for even a live dog is better than a dead lion.” “For the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing. They have no further reward, because the memory of them is forgotten.” Their love and hate and envy have vanished, and they have no share left in anything done under the sun. That is his observation, stated under his limiter, without flinching.

The refrain answers chapter 9 the way it answered chapter 8, now as a command: “Go, eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a cheerful heart, for God has already approved your works.” White garments, oil on the head, and “Enjoy life with your beloved wife all the days of the fleeting life that God has given you under the sun,” because this is your portion. Work gets the same urgency: “Whatever you find to do with your hands, do it with all your might, for in Sheol, where you are going, there is no work or planning or knowledge or wisdom.” Then the chapter's cold splash: “The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong; neither is the bread to the wise, nor the wealth to the intelligent, nor the favor to the skillful. For time and chance happen to all.” Men are snared like fish and birds in an evil time that falls suddenly. And his last exhibit is a small city saved by a poor wise man whom nobody remembered afterward: “Yet no one remembered that poor man.” “Wisdom is better than strength, but the wisdom of the poor man is despised, and his words are not heeded.” Better, and despised, and forgotten: all three in one saying.

title: Remember Your Creator
subtitle: Ecclesiastes 10:1–12:14
description: The last sayings, the ventures of faith, the aging poem, and the book's own conclusion about the whole matter.
paragraphs: The last chapters gather the Teacher's sayings, and chapter 10 opens with a smell: “As dead flies bring a stench to the perfumer’s oil, so a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor.” The fool advertises himself on the road: “Even as the fool walks along the road, his sense is lacking, and he shows everyone that he is a fool.” Under rulers the world turns upside down, and he has seen it: “Folly is appointed to great heights, but the rich sit in lowly positions.” “I have seen slaves on horseback, while princes go on foot like slaves.” If a ruler's temper flares, the counsel is calmness rather than flight, because calmness lays great offenses to rest.

Work and speech fill the rest of the chapter. The ditch digger may fall into his ditch, the wall breacher may meet the snake, and the log splitter endangers himself; work has teeth. “If the axe is dull and the blade unsharpened, more strength must be exerted, but skill produces success.” The wise man's mouth is gracious, “but the lips of a fool consume him,” and the fool multiplies words about a future no one can tell him. Lands are blessed or cursed by their princes' breakfasts: princes feasting at the proper time, for strength, against princes feasting in the morning. The sluggard is back from Proverbs, unchanged: “Through laziness the roof caves in, and in the hands of the idle, the house leaks.” And the feast sayings end with the line quoted more than any other in the chapter: “A feast is prepared for laughter, and wine makes life merry, but money is the answer for everything.” Even private speech is unsafe in his world: “Do not curse the king even in your thoughts, or curse the rich even in your bedroom, for a bird of the air may carry your words, and a winged creature may report your speech.”

Chapter 11 turns the argument into ventures. If nothing can be known, the answer is not paralysis: “Cast your bread upon the waters, for after many days you will find it again.” “Divide your portion among seven, or even eight, for you do not know what disaster may befall the land.” Weather-watchers never plant: “He who watches the wind will fail to sow, and he who observes the clouds will fail to reap.” The path of the wind and the forming of bones in the womb are alike unknowable, and both are God's work. So work both ends of the day: “Sow your seed in the morning, and do not rest your hands in the evening, for you do not know which will succeed, whether this or that, or if both will equally prosper.” Uncertainty, in the Teacher's hands, is a reason to sow twice.

Then the light: “Light is sweet, and it pleases the eyes to see the sun.” A long life is to be rejoiced in, with the dark days remembered because they will be many. Youth gets the book's direct address: “Rejoice, O young man, while you are young, and let your heart be glad in the days of your youth. Walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes,” “but know that for all these things God will bring you to judgment.” Banish sorrow, cast off pain, for youth is fleeting. And the address becomes the book's great command: “Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the days of adversity come and the years approach of which you will say,” “I find no pleasure in them,” The aging poem follows in images: “on the day the keepers of the house tremble and the strong men stoop,” the grinders few, the watchers dim, the doors shut, the mill quiet, “when the almond tree blossoms, the grasshopper loses its spring, and the caper berry shrivels,” “for then man goes to his eternal home and mourners walk the streets.” The end is three breakages and a return: “Remember Him before the silver cord is snapped and the golden bowl is crushed,” “before the dust returns to the ground from which it came and the spirit returns to God who gave it.”

Then the frame closes, and a second voice speaks about the Teacher rather than as him. First his own line returns as the book's last word from his mouth: “Futility of futilities,” “Everything is futile!” Then the epilogue commends him: “Not only was the Teacher wise, but he also taught the people knowledge; he pondered, searched out, and arranged many proverbs.” “The Teacher searched to find delightful sayings and to record accurate words of truth.” The words of the wise, it says, “are like goads, and the anthologies of the masters are like firmly embedded nails driven by a single Shepherd.” A warning rides along for readers of books like this one: “There is no end to the making of many books, and much study wearies the body.” And then the book's own conclusion, quoted as it stands: “When all has been heard, the conclusion of the matter is this: Fear God and keep His commandments, because this is the whole duty of man.” “For God will bring every deed into judgment, along with every hidden thing, whether good or evil.” The Teacher's last word was futility. The book's last word is judgment and fear of God. The seam between them is left exactly where the text leaves it.
